headline: Texas A&M breeds hemp with no detectable THC; seed targeted for 2029
dek: Texas A&M AgriLife Research said on 19 November that its glandless Type V hemp showed none of 18 cannabinoids in lab tests, with field trials due in 2027.
key_points: Texas A&M AgriLife Research announced on 19 November a hemp plant that produced no detectable cannabinoids, including THC, in laboratory testing.
The plants lack the glands on top of trichomes where cannabinoids are made; the team got there by chemical mutation and selection, not gene editing.
The trait is patent-pending and exclusively licensed to Rare Earth Genomics Texas LLC, which sponsored the research.
Seed increases are planned this winter and field trials in 2027 and 2028; AgriLife-bred varieties could reach growers by 2029.
body: Scientists at Texas A&M AgriLife Research say they have bred a hemp plant that makes no detectable cannabinoids at all, THC included. The university announced the result on Thursday 19 November. If it holds up in the field, it removes the risk that has shadowed fibre and grain hemp since the crop became legal: a field that tests over the THC limit and has to be destroyed.

The claim comes from the university's own release and has not yet been tested in field trials. Those are planned for 2027 and 2028. The lead breeder, Russ Jessup, expects seed from AgriLife-bred varieties to be available to producers by 2029.
## What the team did

Cannabinoids are made in trichomes, the tiny hair-like structures on the plant. Each normally carries a gland on top. Other programmes have tried to switch off the genes that build cannabinoids, including by gene editing, and according to Jessup none has removed 100% of THC and other cannabinoids.

The AgriLife team went after the structure instead of the chemistry. Teja Sri Vengala, who began the work as a master's student under Jessup in 2022 and is now lead plant scientist at Rare Earth Genomics, treated hemp seed with ethyl methanesulfonate, a chemical that causes random genetic changes. She then searched thousands of plants for one whose trichomes had no glands.

After self-pollinating those plants, she tested them by high-performance liquid chromatography for 18 cannabinoids. The analysis detected none. Whole-genome sequencing pointed to two candidate genes linked to trichome development that may explain the trait. The team is validating those genes with the university's genomics service and developing molecular markers so breeders can track the trait.

Vengala's calibration of the chemical dose for industrial hemp seed was published in the journal Crops, the release says. Jessup stressed that the method is conventional mutation breeding. In his words, "There's no GMO part to what she did."
## Why growers care

Hemp is legally defined by a THC ceiling of 0.3%. In Texas, a crop that tests above it must be destroyed. That is a manageable risk for a high-value flower crop and a serious one for fibre and grain, where margins are thin and the cannabinoids have no value to the grower.

Jessup gave a concrete example. In 2023, he said, nearly every fibre hemp variety imported from Asia tested above the federal limit in Texas. Those are the only fibre types that grow well in the state, and the losses came close to ending the industry's prospects there. He started the AgriLife hemp programme in 2020.
The new plants are classed as Type V hemp, the category for plants that produce essentially no cannabinoids. A crop with none to measure cannot run hot.
> Most of the hemp debate is about how to count THC. This plant sidesteps the count.
## The timing

The announcement lands in the middle of a federal rewrite of what hemp is. A new federal definition based on total THC, with a cap on THC per container for finished products, is due to take effect on 11 December unless Congress changes it. As we reported on 19 November, the USDA has rewritten hemp crop insurance to match the new THC limits for the 2027 crop year. And as we reported on 17 November, growers face a requirement from 1 January 2027 to use DEA-registered laboratories for compliance testing unless the USDA delays it again.

Each of those rules adds cost or risk to a crop grown for stalks and seed. A plant with no cannabinoids does not remove the paperwork: nothing in the release says Type V hemp would be exempt from testing, and regulators would have to decide that. But it would take away the outcome growers fear most, which is a failed test.

It also points in the opposite direction from the rest of the hemp economy. The businesses fighting the 11 December ban sell cannabinoids. This is hemp with the cannabinoids taken out, aimed at fibre, grain and animal feed.
## Who owns it
The trait is patent-pending and exclusively licensed to Rare Earth Genomics Texas LLC, which sponsored Jessup's research. The release directs anyone who wants the trait to the company.

Jessup said the aim is to make the trait available for others to breed with. Companies, states and countries can cross Type V plants into their own adapted fibre, grain or dual-purpose varieties and reselect for the trait, he said, and government bodies and companies in several countries have already shown interest. He noted that many countries have THC limits stricter than the United States, which widens the market for a zero-cannabinoid plant.

For Texas, the AgriLife team plans its own Type V fibre, grain and dual-purpose varieties. Jessup said no grain hemp from Canada or Europe currently suits the state. He added that hemp grain can be handled with the small-grains equipment many farms already own, and that its omega-3 and omega-6 fatty acid profile could make it useful as livestock and poultry feed.
## What we do not know yet

Several things. "No detectable" depends on the detection limit of the test, which the release does not give. The plants have been tested in a breeding programme, not across seasons, soils and stress conditions, which is where THC surprises usually appear. The trait's stability over generations, and yield and fibre quality in the new lines, are still to be shown. The licence terms and seed price are not public.

The exclusive licence also deserves a note. A single company will control access to a trait that, if it works, many breeders will want. How that licence is priced and shared will shape how fast the trait spreads.
## What to watch

Watch for seed increases this winter and the first field data from the 2027 trials. Watch for peer-reviewed results on the Type V plants themselves, beyond the dosing study already published. Watch whether the USDA or state agriculture departments say how a cannabinoid-free variety would be treated under testing rules. And watch 11 December and 1 January 2027, the two federal dates that set the rules these plants would be grown under.
